common_name: Coccineus Red Valerian (Deep Crimson Jupiter's Beard)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants after the soil has warmed, into lean, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun.

directions: Plant container specimens in spring into poor to average, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; this selected form holds a deeper, more saturated crimson-red flower color than the wild species and comes fairly true from seed if isolated from other Centranthus color forms. Cut plants back hard after the first flush of bloom to encourage rebloom and prevent the sprawling, woody habit that develops on old crowns. It tolerates poor, rocky, or alkaline soils and thrives in gravel gardens, dry stone walls, and coastal plantings where richer soil would cause floppy, weak growth. Deadhead spent flower clusters regularly to extend the bloom season and curb the aggressive self-seeding typical of the species.

common_name: Albus White Red Valerian (White-Flowered Jupiter's Beard)

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into lean, well-drained, alkaline soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in poor to average, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun to light shade; the white form softens the front of a border or gravel garden and combines well with silver-leaved Mediterranean companions like santolina and lavender. Like the species, it flowers best in lean, dry conditions and becomes floppy and short-lived if grown too rich or wet. Shear back after the first bloom flush to tidy the plant and prompt a second round of flowers into late summer. It self-seeds readily, but seedlings often revert toward the pink-red species type, so remove off-color volunteers if a pure white stand is desired.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring or fall into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this cultivar does not come true from seed and must be propagated by cuttings.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown specimens in average to lean, sharply drained soil in full sun; 'Bowles's Mauve' is a sterile hybrid of uncertain parentage that produces spikes of rich purple-mauve flowers held above gray-green foliage almost continuously from late winter through fall in mild climates. Because it sets little to no seed, energy that would otherwise go to seed production instead fuels an exceptionally long bloom season, making it one of the most floriferous of all perennial wallflowers. Plants are relatively short-lived, typically fading after three to four years, so take softwood cuttings periodically to keep a young generation coming along. Avoid heavy, wet, or poorly drained soils, which shorten its lifespan further and encourage root and crown rot.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)
